awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Collaborative Research: Examining Critical Infrastructure and Protective Decision-Making During 14-15 March 2025 Multi-State Nocturnal Tornado Outbreak
awd_abstract_narration:
The objective of this Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project is to collect time-sensitive data on how housing infrastructure, risk perception, and warning communication influence people’s ability to take protective action during nighttime tornadoes. On 14-15 March 2025, a deadly outbreak of nocturnal tornadoes occurred across the Midwestern United States. When tornado disasters occur at night, they significantly increase fatality and injury rates, as they are difficult for the public to receive warnings and take protective action, as many are often asleep in homes that may lack adequate wind-resistant features or safe sheltering options. By integrating tools and methods from civil engineering and the social and behavioral sciences, the project aims to advance interdisciplinary knowledge about nighttime tornado sheltering vulnerability and decision-making processes.

Using a convergent mixed-methods design and guided by the Protective Action Decision Model (PADM), the project conducts engineering assessments of wind damage across residential housing types and collects survey data on how households responded to the tornado outbreak. Project findings provide new understanding of converging social, behavioral, and built environment factors that facilitate or hinder effective protective action during nighttime tornado threats and will inform public warning systems, safe housing guidance, and emergency planning. Results are broadly shared with weather forecasters, emergency managers, and researchers as well as supporting student training and education across engineering and social science programs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Project Outcomes Report

During the overnight hours between 14-15 March 2025, a historic and deadly outbreak of nocturnal tornadoes occurred across the Midwestern region of United States (U.S.), producing catastrophic damage, particularly in various counties of Missouri, that resulted in 44 fatalities and more than 247 injuries. When tornado hazards occur at night, they significantly increase public fatality and injury rates, as they are difficult for weather and emergency response infrastructure to warn for and difficult for the public to receive and respond to nocturnal tornado warnings, as many households and their social networks are often sleeping in their homes. Furthermore, the Midwest contains a high percentage of populations living in housing structures with inadequate wind-resistant materials, making them more susceptible to damage and more dangerous for those needing shelter during nocturnal tornado threats.

Intellectual Merit: The project generated interdisciplinary knowledge about how structural characteristics of the built environment interacted with social and behavioral factors to shape vulnerability and protective decision-making during nocturnal tornadoes. Guided by the Protective Action Decision Model (PADM), the study included structural engineering assessments of residential infrastructure and social science data on household warning reception, decision-making, and sheltering responses during the March 14–15, 2025, nocturnal tornado outbreak. Specifically, the project advanced understanding of: (1) the structural wind vulnerability of urban and rural housing infrastructure during a nocturnal tornado outbreak; and (2) the social, behavioral, and built environment factors that facilitated or hindered effective protective action during nocturnal tornado events.

Our engineering teams assessed more than 400 damaged structures across eight communities in Missouri and Arkansas using a combination of satellite imagery, drone-based aerial reconnaissance, radar observations, and door-to-door field assessments. Findings showed that damage severity generally increased with tornado intensity and proximity to the tornado path. However, the study also documented substantial variation in damage among buildings exposed to similar tornado conditions, suggesting that construction characteristics and structural details influence building performance beyond tornado intensity alone. Engineering assessments identified roof systems, roof-to-wall connections, wall cladding, and fastening systems as recurring points of structural failure. Wood-frame residential structures experienced higher levels of severe damage and destruction than masonry structures, highlighting opportunities to improve tornado resilience through enhanced construction practices and adoption of updated building codes. Findings also indicated that some relatively modern residential structures remained vulnerable to severe damage during strong tornadoes, emphasizing the need for continued evaluation of building practices in tornado-prone regions. The project further demonstrated that satellite imagery can help identify severe tornado damage paths and support rapid post-disaster damage assessments across large geographic areas.

The project also surveyed 1,001 residents from Missouri, Arkansas, and Illinois who received tornado warnings during the outbreak. Survey findings identified several factors associated with protective action. Residents with access to multiple warning sources, higher perceptions of tornado risk, and greater confidence in the effectiveness of protective actions were more likely to seek shelter during the March nocturnal tornado outbreak. In contrast, respondents who reported fewer warning cues, lower perceptions of risk, and lower confidence in protective actions were less likely to take protective action. Participants also identified barriers to protective action, including being asleep when tornado warnings were issued and experiencing limited warning reception due to power outages and loss of cellular service during the event. These findings highlight the importance of having multiple warning sources that can awaken residents, particularly during overnight hours when residents are asleep and severe weather may disrupt communication infrastructure. Together, these findings highlight that effective overnight tornado warning systems depend not only on the issuance of accurate warnings, but also on residents’ ability to receive warnings while asleep, understand their risk, and have access to structurally safe sheltering options. Increasing access to warning sources capable of awakening residents, strengthening nighttime household preparedness, and improving public understanding of nocturnal tornado risk may enhance protective responses during overnight tornado events. Results also suggest that warning systems that can awaken residents and operate independently of cellular networks or household electricity, such as battery-powered NOAA weather radios, may provide an additional layer of protection during nocturnal tornado events. Collectively, this work advances understanding of tornado-induced structural vulnerability and key factors that support or prevent household warning reception and response during nocturnal tornado threats.

Broader Impacts: This project supported three graduate students from two universities and provided training in survey development and analysis, as well as engineering damage assessments, experience in academic writing, presentation, and interdisciplinary collaboration among engineers, atmospheric scientists, and social scientists. The research team has delivered four presentations at academic and professional conferences to disseminate findings to scientific and practitioner audiences. Two manuscripts are in preparation for submission to peer-reviewed journals. Data generated from the datasets (de-identified) will be archived and made publicly available through the DesignSafe data repository to support open science and future research.
